title: Instantaneous Velocity and Acceleration
notes: **Average velocity** tells you the overall displacement over a time interval; **instantaneous velocity** tells you the velocity at one exact instant — defined as the limit of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero.

**Mathematical definition of instantaneous velocity:** v = lim_{Δt→0} Δs/Δt = ds/dt. As Δt → 0, the ratio Δs/Δt approaches the instantaneous rate of change of position with time — the derivative of position with respect to time.

**Graphical interpretation of velocity:** On a displacement-time (s-t) graph, the slope of the tangent line at any point equals the instantaneous velocity at that instant. A steeper tangent means higher speed.
**Instantaneous acceleration:** Defined as a = lim_{Δt→0} Δv/Δt = dv/dt. On a velocity-time (v-t) graph, the slope of the tangent at a point gives the instantaneous acceleration at that instant.

**Why the limit matters:** Without taking the limit, Δs/Δt is only an average over a finite time interval and misses what happens within that interval. The limit extracts the local behavior — the true speed and direction at one exact moment.
**Units of velocity and acceleration:** Velocity has units of length/time (m/s in SI). Acceleration has units of length/time² (m/s² in SI). From the definitions: [v] = [L T⁻¹], [a] = [L T⁻²].

**Relation between velocity and acceleration graphs:** The slope of an s-t graph gives velocity; the slope of a v-t graph gives acceleration. Conversely, the area under an a-t graph gives the change in velocity: Δv = ∫a dt, and the area under a v-t graph gives displacement: Δs = ∫v dt.

**Positive and negative acceleration:** The sign of acceleration relative to velocity matters. If v and a have the same sign, the object is speeding up. If v and a have opposite signs, the object is slowing down (decelerating).

**Higher derivatives:** The time derivative of acceleration is called jerk (j = da/dt = d³s/dt³), and higher derivatives are called snap, crackle, and pop. Jerk is important in engineering design (elevator smoothness, roller coaster rides).

**Chain rule forms:** If position is given as a function of position-dependent velocity, a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v(dv/dx). This is useful when acceleration is expressed as a function of position rather than time: a(x) = v·dv/dx.
**Constant acceleration equations:** When a is constant, v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at², and v² = u² + 2as, where u is initial velocity and v is final velocity.

**Terminal velocity:** When drag force balances gravity (mg = kv for linear drag or mg = kv² for quadratic drag), acceleration becomes zero and velocity reaches a constant terminal value. d²s/dt² = 0 means the s-t graph becomes linear.
confusion: Many students think instantaneous velocity is an 'approximation' — it is NOT. It is an exact value obtained by the mathematical limit process. The instantaneous velocity at an instant is as precise as the slope of the tangent line to the curve.

Velocity is a vector (speed + direction), acceleration is also a vector. An object moving in a circle at constant speed has nonzero acceleration (centripetal), even though its speed is constant — because velocity direction changes.

'Deceleration' is not the opposite of 'acceleration' — deceleration occurs when acceleration and velocity have opposite signs. An object moving left (negative v) and speeding up has positive acceleration (a points right) if the speed is increasing.

On a velocity-time graph, areas above the time axis are positive (velocity in +x direction); areas below are negative (velocity in −x direction). The TOTAL area gives displacement; the sum of |areas| gives total distance traveled.

The derivative ds/dt requires calculus — many students try to compute instantaneous velocity by plugging into v = Δs/Δt with small numbers instead of taking the limit. This introduces rounding errors and is not the correct mathematical procedure.
practice: The position of a particle is given by x(t) = 3t³ - 10t² + 6t + 20, where x is in meters and t in seconds. Find (a) velocity at t=2s, (b) acceleration at t=2s. Solution: (a) v = dx/dt = 9t² - 20t + 6. At t=2: v = 9(4) - 20(2) + 6 = 36 - 40 + 6 = 2 m/s. (b) a = dv/dt = 18t - 20. At t=2: a = 36 - 20 = 16 m/s².

A particle's acceleration is a(t) = 6t + 4 m/s². If the initial velocity v(0) = 5 m/s and initial position x(0) = 3 m, find (a) velocity function v(t), (b) position function x(t), (c) velocity at t=3s. Solution: (a) v(t) = ∫a dt = ∫(6t+4)dt = 3t² + 4t + C. At t=0, v=5 → C=5. So v(t) = 3t² + 4t + 5. (b) x(t) = ∫v dt = ∫(3t²+4t+5)dt = t³ + 2t² + 5t + D. At t=0, x=3 → D=3. So x(t) = t³ + 2t² + 5t + 3. (c) v(3) = 3(9) + 4(3) + 5 = 27+12+5 = 44 m/s.

The position of a simple harmonic oscillator is x(t) = 5 cos(3t + π/4), in meters. Find the velocity and acceleration at t=0.5 s. Solution: v(t) = dx/dt = -5·3·sin(3t + π/4) = -15sin(3t + π/4). At t=0.5: 3(0.5)+π/4 = 1.5+0.785 = 2.285 rad. v = -15sin(2.285) = -15×0.755 = -11.32 m/s. a(t) = dv/dt = -45cos(3t + π/4). a = -45cos(2.285) = -45×(-0.656) = 29.52 m/s².

Given the velocity-time graph of a car: v(t) increases linearly from 0 to 20 m/s in the first 10 s, then stays constant at 20 m/s for the next 10 s, then decreases linearly to 0 in the final 10 s. Find (a) acceleration at t=5s, (b) acceleration at t=15s, (c) acceleration at t=25s. Solution: (a) t=5s is in the first interval (0-10s), slope = 20/10 = 2 m/s², so a = 2 m/s². (b) t=15s is in the constant region (10-20s), slope = 0, so a = 0 m/s². (c) t=25s is in the third interval (20-30s), slope = (0-20)/10 = -2 m/s², so a = -2 m/s².

A rocket's altitude is given by y(t) = 8t² - 15t³/2 for t ≥ 0, in meters. Find (a) velocity at t=2 s, (b) acceleration at t=2 s, (c) when does it hit the ground? Solution: (a) v = dy/dt = 16t - (45/2)t². At t=2: v = 32 - 45 = -13 m/s (moving downward). (b) a = dv/dt = 16 - 45t. At t=2: a = 16 - 90 = -74 m/s². (c) Ground hit: y=0 → 8t² - (15/2)t³ = 0 → t²(8 - 15t/2) = 0 → t=0 (launch) or t = 16/15 = 1.067 s (landing).
universalFacts: Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position and requires calculus to define precisely. The concept was formalized in the 17th century by Newton and Leibniz independently.
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, making it the second derivative of position: a(t) = d²x/dt². Similarly, jerk is the third derivative: j(t) = d³x/dt³.

In physics, 'average' quantities are defined over finite intervals; 'instantaneous' quantities are defined in the limit of a vanishingly small interval. The instantaneous value represents the local behavior of the function.
The fundamental theorem of calculus connects differentiation (instantaneous rates) and integration (accumulated quantities): ∫v(t)dt from t₁ to t₂ gives displacement, and d/dt[∫v(t)dt] = v(t).

For motion in a straight line, speed is the absolute value of velocity: |v| = |dx/dt|. An object can have negative velocity (moving backward) and positive acceleration (speeding up in the negative direction).
